utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, good afternoon to all. Before we get on with the trial, there is a clarification that I still owe you all, something I said on Friday. Mr. Smith said something about the two of us getting together after the hearing on Friday. I made a mistake during my cross-examination, and I would like to point this out, so that everybody is aware of it. The error will be perfectly clear once the witness is here, the person we mentioned as D during our cross-examination, so during my cross-examination. I asked the witness whether it was true that he had beaten D. And then D gave two statements where he said that last week's person had beaten somebody else, but not him, merely claiming that the witness had participated in the beating. That was an error on my part, an error that I had made during my preparation for cross-examination. It was never in my interests to claim that this witness was beating that man, but what is certain is that the person we referred to as D said what he said. I think soon enough we shall have a chance to confront other witnesses with these allegations. That's all I wanted to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will have the witness in then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that is given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith will now have some questions for you. Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, can you please state your name and your age, please?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Vilim Karlovic. I am 35 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where were you born and raised?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: In Zagreb, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what's your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I'm an ethnic Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you did your schooling in Zagreb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you ever serve in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you ever serve in the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when did you join up with the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: In early August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how old were you when you joined?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Just about to turn 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why did you join the army?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Because my home country was under attack. I wanted to contribute to my home country's defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say your home country, you're referring to Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who was attacking it?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: The JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you joined up, where were they attacking in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: The most difficult situation was in Eastern Slavonia, as far as I remember, also the area known as Lika, and the Croatian south. As well as Banja.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what about Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I did say that. I included that in the category that I described as Eastern Slavonia. Eastern Croatia, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after you joined up in early August, did you undertake any training?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were trained for two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were you deployed anywhere after the training?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were first sent to the surroundings of Petrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where is Petrinja?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: It's a town about 50 kilometres south of Zagreb in an area known as Banja.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long were you in Petrinja for, and what did you do there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Between 50 [as interpreted] and 20 days. We held positions there in a village called Petski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, I notice the transcript at the very end may have misrecorded 15 for 50, in the number of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think you're right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'll clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, it was between 15 and 20 days, not 50 and 20; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after Petrinja, where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: We returned to Zagreb, and stayed just outside Zagreb on a hill called Medvednice. We were securing some sort of a warehouse there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And at some point in that year did you go to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was right after that we went to Vukovar; more specifically, on the 30th of September that same year, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in Vukovar for? For about what period of time?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed there up until the fall of Vukovar. More specifically, until the 22nd of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after the 22nd of November, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I was taken to Sremska Mitrovica as a prisoner. I was taken to Sremska Mitrovica's prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who took you as a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: The JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long were you in the prison the Sremska Mitrovica for?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after you left Sremska Mitrovica prison, where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Back to Croatia, Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you continue to serve in the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you involved in any further combat operations after 1992?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were you involved in combat operations in Dubrovnik and in 1993 and 1994 at Zadar and in 1995 in Western Slavonia in Operation Storm and Flash?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when did you leave the army?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Early in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And is it correct that your occupation now is a builder?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I actually own a construction company.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you have a large family to support now; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I guess you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I would like to go back now to the 30th of September, 1991 when you were deployed in Vukovar. How many of you were deployed in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: The group with which I arrived comprised 21 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you give the Court an indication of the brigade and the company and the battalion that you belonged to at that time?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I belonged to the 1st Brigade, 4th Battalion, 3rd Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And this group which you belonged to, who was the commander of that group?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: The commander was Tihomir Perkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were there any deputy commanders in that unit?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The deputy was Josip Nemec.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you also play a command role in that unit?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had 10 people under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And at the time that you were deployed to Vukovar, what information did you have as to what was occurring in Vukovar before you got there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we knew that Vukovar was surrounded and was being attacked by strong forces of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: At that stage were you only aware of the JNA surrounding Vukovar? Or were you aware of any other types of units?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: We knew that in addition to the JNA there were the Serbian TO, the volunteers, the reservists, and we also knew about a number of Chetnik volunteers' units fighting alongside with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what were your unit's instructions when you were deployed there? What were you told to do?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: We were first sent to the silo in Vukovar. We guarded the banks of the Danube in a bid to prevent a possible crossing by the Serb forces on the other side. Later we were reassigned to other positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that when you were deployed that you believed or you had information that Vukovar was surrounded by the JNA and other groups. When you got to Vukovar, what was the case? Was it surrounded or was that incorrect?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The silos in Vukovar, about how far away from the Danube river are they?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we can say it's right at the Danube. The distance may be between 100 and 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How did you get to the silos?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: On foot. We walked from Bogdanovci. We walked through the cornfields and reached Luzac. It was from Luzac that we eventually reached the silo in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you got to Vukovar, what was happening in the town?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: One could tell immediately that the town had suffered severe shelling. There was no one to be seen anywhere. Everyone was in their cellars. You could tell that this was war for real.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How long were you at the silos before you moved to another position?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: For about 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Whilst you were at the silos, did you see or were you involved in any combat?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't involved myself, aside from the fighting from the silo, the positions there. As for the silo itself, it was just shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The silo was shelled on one occasion or more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Every day. Several shells every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to say who was doing the shelling and where it was coming from?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: We knew that some of the shells were coming from across the Danube, from Serbia. More specifically, from Vojvodina. This was something that we were sure about, aside from that, the shells could potentially have come from just about anywhere. But our conclusion was that it was the JNA shelling us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when your unit arrived in Vukovar, did it report to anyone else higher up?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: What I know is that my own commander and his deputy reported to the town's commander. It was Mr. Dedakovic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the weaponry that your unit had, what was that?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: We had small arms and some light rocket launchers, disposable ones. The sort you could only use once. On top of that we had a number of hand-grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why were you moved from the silos to another location in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: There was no hand-to-hand combat around the silo. And the general belief was that we would be more useful at other positions where the town was under threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Whilst you were at the silos, did there appear to be any military reason as to why the silos were being shelled?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Probably. The silo straddled an elevation and it was actually quite tall. It could be used as a very good observation post. It also had storage rooms dug in the ground where one could store ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was ammunition stored in those silos, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The other locations that you were deployed to in Vukovar, where were they?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: We were deployed to Prvomajska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where is Prvomajska Street? Where is that in relation to, say, the Vuka River?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: It's north of Prvomajska Street, the River Vuka. In relation to the barracks, Prvomajska Street was north of the barracks and the River Vuka to the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you refer to the barracks, you're referring to the JNA barracks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you got to this new position, what was happening there militarily?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: There was a true hand-to-hand war going on there. We were attacked every day by the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were you able to see the enemy and identify what groups they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who was it? Who was the enemy?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: The JNA. The JNA was the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what type of hand-to-hand war was it? Was it along a front line, or was it not so discernible?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: When we got there, there still was some for several days, but then very shortly after that they cut us off in many positions. So that it could be said that from the beginning of November there was no proper defence line any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How long did you stay in that position?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: At the positions in Prvomajska Street, actually we moved from there. I don't know how long we remained in Prvomajska Street. And then after the 1st of November we were in retreat and then onwards. When I'm referring to retreat, I mean that we kept moving closer and closer to the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the situation by the middle of November 1991?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, it was quite chaotic. In essence, it was clear to us that it was a matter of days when we would have to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you finally surrender?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About what date was that, and how did that happen?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: As for myself, I can say that I surrendered on the 20th of November, which is when the JNA captured me in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When did you arrive at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: On the 17th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what about other members of your unit. Did they arrive with you on that day, or had they been there before?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were several soldiers of mine who had been wounded earlier. They were in the hospital. And some didn't even go to the hospital with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What happened to the ones that didn't got to the hospital? Where did they go?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where they went, because when my group was deployed to Prvomajska Street, we did not remain all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many members of your unit had been wounded and were at the hospital by the time you got there on the 17th of November?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: As for the hospital, I remember some six or seven people who had been wounded and then hospitalised, were staying in the hospital. I know that two of them had been transferred from the hospital to Borovo Komerc prior to that, because some of the wounded were treated there as well. So that I was aware of some, let's say, eight people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why did you go to the hospital on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: For the simple reason that that was the only place where I could expect some degree of safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Why did you not surrender from your combat positions?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, because we did not have any combat positions any longer. Second, I felt that if I surrendered with a large group, I would fare better. I was afraid to surrender on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you went to the hospital, were you wearing your uniform, and did you still have your weapon?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have my weapon any longer. We were not allowed to go to the hospital with our weapons. Therefore, I had left it in a house in the vicinity of the hospital. As for my uniform, I think that I took it off at the police station, or in the vicinity of the police station in a building there, because the police station had already been destroyed. When I reached the hospital, I wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you see other men seeking refuge in the hospital with their weapons whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see anybody entering the hospital seeking shelter there with weapons. At least I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that you believe that the JNA had surrounded the town before you got to Vukovar, and also that the Serbian TOs, volunteers, reservists, and Chetniks were fighting with the JNA. When were you able -- or were you able to see what types of uniforms or not these people were wearing, these different groups you referred to?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I can give you the following description: The JNA mostly wore olive-green uniforms. On their helmets and caps they had a five-pointed star. When I say the JNA, I'm referring both to the regular troops and reservists. Members of the Territorial Defence wore similar attire to the JNA, but they also had the Serbian flag symbols on their clothing. The Chetniks stood out the most. They did not have a standard uniform. They wore both military uniforms and civilian clothes. And they mostly wore the head-wear that I will describe as fur hats, and also folk caps with a cockade on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And are you able to compare the way that, say, the regular JNA and the reserve JNA were dressed to, say, the Chetniks in terms of their neatness?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: It is clear that the JNA troops respected the order, looked orderly. The Chetniks looked unkempt; they had long hair, were unshaven, had long beards, and this is how they differed from the JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was there any which that you could determine the difference between a regular JNA soldier and a reservist? Is there any characteristic difference that you could draw between the two? Because you said the uniforms were similar or the same.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I have to be frank and say that it was quite difficult to discern them. All I can say is that the reservists, as a rule, were older than conscripts or regular troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that the regular JNA and reservists would wear olive-green uniforms. Did they ever wear camouflage uniforms, are you aware?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they also wore camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what colour camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: That was a uniform in various shades of green, from light green to dark green.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you mentioned to me before we testified that you have a slight eye condition where it's difficult for you to determine differing shades of certain colours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's not that I have a problems with my eyesight, it's just that I can't tell some colour shades.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I would ask that -- Your Honours, that we play Exhibit 219. It's a video clip of some soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, I would like you to have a look at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: This video clip is in Sanction, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, I would like you to have a look at this video clip, it's quite short. It shows some soldiers in differing and varying uniforms. And after the clip is played, we will show you some still shots, and I would like you to describe what groups you believe these people belonged to, from your experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I would ask that we go to the clip, a still at five seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you have seen that video clip before; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: This is at the five-second mark of this exhibit. Witness, looking at those men you see in the photograph, say the person on the right-hand side, from your experience in Vukovar, what group do you believe he belongs to?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I would categorise them as a Chetnik group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if we look at the man on the left-hand side, with the helmet, what group would he belong to?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: In my view, he could have been a reservist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if we can go to the still at 10 seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we look at the man on the left-hand side in the camouflage uniform, are you able to say what group he would belong to?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I would consider him to be a member of the Serbian TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why would you say that?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I can see that he wears no insignia, so it's hard to place him in any group, but it is obvious that he has somewhat longer hair and a nondescript uniform, so he could have been a member of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you recognise anyone in that still by name?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I don't recognise anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can tender that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "that"?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The still.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This particular still. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number 289.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if we can move to the 12-second mark, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You didn't tender the five second. Did you want to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It also will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 290, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we could move to the 12-second mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, looking at that photograph with the man on the left-hand side wearing the beret, are you able to say what group he would belong to?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I would categorise him as a member of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you recognise anyone in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: No. No one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I seek to tender that still, Your Honour, at the 12-second mark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 291, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if we can go to the 13-second mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think we can leave it at that. I've finished with the exhibit now. Thank you. If we can show Exhibit 156 on the screen, please. And if we can enlarge it one further level, thank you. If we can move it to the left. A little bit further to the right. If we stop there, thank you. And if we can move it up the screen a little, please. Sorry down the screen. Further. Thank you. If we stop there, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, looking at this map on the screen, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I do. I can see that this is Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you see the Vukovar river running through the centre of the town?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you also see the location of the silos, or the general area where your position was when you first arrived in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, I would ask that the location where the silos were, or are, can you mark that with an A, please?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And with a B could you mark the general location of the second location you went to, Prvomajska Street -- I've probably mispronounced that. I believe it's the 1st of May Street in English.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I seek to tender that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be exhibit number 292, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, if we can go back to the hospital now, when you arrived there on the 17th of November what was the atmosphere like in the hospital, and what did you see there? If you can give us an overall impression, please.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, there were many people, because people had arrived to the hospital from shelters and other places. So there was a lot of commotion there, and in everybody's face you could see fear. Fear of what was ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you stay in one part of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In a basement in a part of the hospital. Rather, it was a corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that you believed you surrendered on the 20th of November. Does that mean that you were in the hospital for at least a couple of days before you left the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, towards the evening on the 17th I arrived in the hospital. So I believe that I stayed there for three nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what did you do for those three days -- or three nights and two days?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't do anything. I stayed in the basement, in the corridor, the entire time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who was in the corridor with you?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: There were some civilians, some wounded persons, also women, children.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were there many other soldiers like yourself that had left their weapons outside and come into the hospital, into the basement with you?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see anybody where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And before you arrived at the hospital were you told, or did you know, what was going to happen at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I knew that somebody from the hospital was negotiating the surrender. I also knew that the hospital, together with everybody staying in there, was supposed to surrender to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the night before you left the hospital, or the day before, the 19th of November, did anything significant happen that day?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th, in the evening, I saw the JNA members for the first time enter the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many entered the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how many entered the hospital, but in the area that I was able to see, some seven to eight men passed through the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you see them do anything else, apart from passing through the corridor?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't do anything. In fact, they seemed to be quite calm or peace-loving.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The following day, the following morning, on the 20th, can you tell the Court what happened at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime at around 9.00 or 10.00, we were issued an order to leave the hospital and go to the opposite side. The order applied to everyone who was lightly wounded and could walk. And that's what happened. We left through the back door and went behind the hospital where we lined up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who issued that order?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: What I was able to see, the people who issued orders to us were the JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you were lined up, what happened?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Once we were lined up, they started frisking us. They searched everyone who was in the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who was doing the searching and about how many were doing it?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: The JNA soldiers. There were about 10 to 15 soldiers searching the entire group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was there anyone in charge of these soldiers at that stage? Did you see anyone in charge of them, or that appeared to be in charge?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I remember two men there who were in charge of this whole operation, frisking people and separating people off. And there were some ordinary soldiers there doing everything that these other two men were telling them to do. The important thing is, they all belonged to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What about other groups that you have referred to, like Chetniks and Territorial Defence? Were they at the hospital as well or not?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I did not see any Chetniks inside the hospital. I saw several TO men inside. As for what was going on outside in the courtyard, the Chetniks were nearby. So were the TO. But they were banned from taking part in the frisking and separating off of our group, the group that had just been brought outside the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the two men that you said were in charge of the whole operation of frisking people and separating people, do you know who they were? Do you know either of their names?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After you were frisked and searched, where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: We were taken to the buses and told to get on the buses. We started driving on these buses through the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How many buses were there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Five buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And on the bus you got on, how many others got on with you?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: The buses were full. A bus can hold between 50 and 55 people, so that would be your number, in relation to any one single bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the people that were placed on the buses, were they men or women, or were they a mix?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I remember there were men only on my bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And these men, do you know whether they were soldiers or civilians or patients? Are you able to say who they were?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part they were wounded from the hospital. That group included both soldiers and civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was there anyone guarding the bus that you were on?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: There were two soldiers in my bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you say what type of soldiers they were?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I know for a fact that one of them was a regular JNA soldier. I'm not sure about the other. That is, I'm not sure whether he was a regular soldier or a reservist. He struck me as slightly older than the other one, the one of whom I was sure was a JNA regular soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Where were these two soldiers sitting on your bus, or standing?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: They were standing at the front of the bus, facing us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were you sitting -- well, where were you sitting on the bus?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I was sitting towards the front, just behind the driver on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And these two soldiers, were they in front of you or behind you?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: In front of me, facing me. Facing us all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to say how long it took from leaving the hospital to being separated, searched and placed on the bus, and then the buses leaving, about how long that -- that whole process took?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Probably took about an hour or so. Perhaps even longer. It's been so many years, but if I had to put money on it, I would say about one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that there was two people that appeared to be in charge of this frisking and searching process. Was there anyone else in authority there other than these two people?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if anybody in particular was in charge, but I did see one particular man turn up at one point. He was yelling at a sergeant there. I heard him yelling at this other man, telling him to get on with it and not just stand there and waste time. It was this yelling that drew my attention to that person being there. It was later on that I found out who that person was. I didn't know at all at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And perhaps if you can describe this particular man, what he was wearing and his build, generally?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I only caught a very short glimpse of this man. I remember that he was taller than me. He was wearing camouflage uniform, and what struck me in particular about him was the moustache.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said --

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember if he had a cap on or not. I just know that it was no helmet, that much is certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said you later found out who this person was. Who was it? Who did you believe it to be?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: This was Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how did you find that out later?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Every year footage covering the fall of Vukovar would be shown on Croatian television. Mr. Sljivancanin was shown quite a lot on these occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you know the names of any of the people that were placed on your bus?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I know about one man who was in my brigade, Ivan Gruber. I'm not from Vukovar myself, and for this reason it was very hard, if impossible, to know anybody else's names.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Could you say this person's name again, the surname, please?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Ivan Gruber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was he injured or not?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In his stomach, in his arm -- or, rather, in his shoulder, and his fist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Of the 50 or so who were on your bus, could you say about how many of them were wounded?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Now that I think back, I think all of them were wounded. How many exactly, that would be really hard to say. I can't say, but I guess over 90 per cent of all the people there. I was wounded myself, but it was negligible. It was just a very slight injury, if compared to some others there who had to use crutches and had their heads bandaged all over. I even saw a man on the bus there who was missing a leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you got on the bus, were you told by the guards, those two soldiers you referred to, where you were going, or by anyone else?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody told us anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where did the buses go?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: They drove us through the town first. Eventually we reached the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what happened when you got to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: The buses were parked in a semicircle of sorts. They kept us waiting there between one and a half and two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when the buses arrived at the barracks, were there any people in the barracks when you first got there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you describe how many were there, and what they were wearing, and who you thought they were?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: When I say "people," what I mean is the enemy, the soldiers who happened to be in the barracks when our buses arrived. There were JNA soldiers there, there were TO men there, as well as Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What about the number of them? Can you give us an impression as to whether there was a few or a lot? And can you try and provide some sort of figure, if you can?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I will try to express this numerically. There must have been between 60 and 70 in that courtyard. The important thing, however, is there was a lot of coming and going. The turnover of their men in that courtyard was quite significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When the buses were parked, what were these -- what were these soldiers doing, this group of people doing?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: The TO men and the Chetniks spent most of their time insulting people and swearing. They would get on the buses and wanted to take some people off. As for the JNA soldiers, they were guarding us, they were guarding our buses. After some time, however, people started to be taken off the buses, and this was -- this procedure was based on some lists that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was anyone taken off your bus?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember whether anyone was actually taken off my bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you explain how this procedure that was based on lists worked? In relation to your bus.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Two soldiers got on the bus. One of them had a list, which he used to call out people's names. I can't remember whether anybody from my bus was taken off. We did notice, however, that people were taken off the other buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: These two soldiers, can you describe what group you would place them in?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what about the two JNA soldiers that were on the bus that came with you from the hospital, what were they doing during this time that you were at the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: They were guarding us, in actual fact. The Chetniks and the TO men were kept from entering the buses. We even felt safe at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that your bus had two JNA soldiers that came with you from the Vukovar Hospital. Can you say whether the other buses had JNA soldiers guarding them from the Vukovar Hospital as well, or are you unable to say?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I can't even remember that. I can only conclude that there were, based on the fact that there was some on my bus. That should, I assume, lead me to conclude that there were some on the other buses too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you see people being taken off other buses?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many people did you see being taken off?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: About 15 people, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you see what happened to these people once they were taken off?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: First they were beaten as they were being taken from the buses to another place. They were being beaten, for the most part, by the Chetniks and the TO men. They moved these people to a sixth bus that was there. It was an olive-drab bus and it was parked beside our buses to the right of where our buses were parked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: At the barracks did there appear to be anyone in charge of these JNA, TOs, Chetniks you saw there, or not?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Outside in the courtyard I noticed that there was a group of people who were consulted. I saw soldiers approach them, and I realised that these were people who obviously enjoyed some degree of authority, but I didn't really notice their ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know what type of soldiers they were?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Whilst these people were threatening the others on the buses, can you tell the Court what atmosphere existed in the bus? How were you feeling and what was the mood in the bus?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in one word, fear. Fear, uncertainty. As simple as that. We could feel an enormous sense of hatred directed at us which, in a way, I could understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why is it that could you understand that?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: We had been locked in a war against each other, that's why.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that you were at the JNA barracks for about an hour to an hour and a half; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. More, perhaps, if anything. But what you have just suggested sounds about right. We were certainly there for at least that long.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where did you go from the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: We first took a road and eventually we reached this farm called Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What about the other buses, where were they?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: All five buses went to the same place, it's just I can't remember what happened to that sixth bus, or where they ended up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did any other vehicles go with the buses to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I remember a military vehicle ahead of us, ahead of the first bus. I remember there was a military vehicle there, and I seem to remember that it was a Pinzgauer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you able to see who was in that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what about behind the buses, were there any vehicles travelling behind?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The two JNA soldiers that left with you from the Vukovar Hospital, where were they when you were heading to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: They were with us on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Had you ever been to Ovcara before?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How did you find out that you were taken to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I learned a little later. When I was rescued, I heard where it was that they had taken us to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you got to Ovcara, can you tell the Court what you saw?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: People were being taken off the buses and led towards this big hangar. At the hangar entrance, there were soldiers. They were stripping people of any valuables, even some of the clothes, and hitting them. This was what they called a gauntlet. After that, people were led into the hangar where they were beaten again. The buses were searched one by one.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, the buses were emptied one by one.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: And then in a column people walked into the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that might be a good place to break. It's coming up to 1545.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you then. We will resume by five past 4.00. We will have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, before we had the break you told the Court what you saw when you first arrived at Ovcara hangar. You talked about the buses parking, the people coming off the buses, and being beaten in a gauntlet and then being beaten inside the hangar. You said that the people were taken off the buses one by one. Where was your bus parked in relation to the others?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: As I was in the penultimate bus, which is to say in the fourth bus, I was a bit further away from the entrance into the hangar in the column behind other buses near the path leading to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you see people being taken off the first bus, or was it only as people were taken off the first and the second bus that you were able to see these beatings in the gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, one could see that. I could see that. Everybody could see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how many people were doing the beating in this gauntlet before the men were placed into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: There must have been at least 30 people participating in the beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you describe whether any of these people doing the beatings appeared to have belonged to any particular military unit or group?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. One could see that the Chetniks and TO men particularly took part in it, but also the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Before you got to the gauntlet, can you -- are you able to say whether you saw anyone in particular being beaten? Could you identify anyone in particular?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I remember Zeljko Major. I saw him pass through the gauntlet and being beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: He was a man from my unit who had arrived together with me in Vukovar and who was wounded in his shoulder and arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said the people were being beaten as they got off the buses. Was everyone being beaten, or was it select -- just a select few from the people coming off the buses?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Everybody was beaten, whoever got off the bus, because the gauntlet was positioned in such a way as to ensure that everybody had to pass through the gauntlet and be beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how long were individuals beaten for before they were placed in the hangar, and can you tell the Court how they were beaten?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: People would get off the bus and go on the road, and then the JNA soldiers would release several people at a time and direct them towards the hangar. They would go in groups of five to six. In the gauntlet they had to take out all of their personal documents, money, jewellery. And then they would be beaten, beaten before they started doing that, and they would continue doing that while being beaten, and they would throw their belongings on the ground. And then the beating would continue after that. Following that they would enter the hangar. And then a new group of five to six persons would arrive, and they would be subjected to the same procedure. As for the beatings and the way that they beat us in the gauntlet, they used rifle-butt, wooden sticks or poles. I even saw one man use a chain. They would also use their hands, feet, practically anything they could get their hands on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to say about how long it took to unload one of the buses, or each of the buses, from the time that they left the bus, to all of them being placed in the hangar for each bus?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: In my view, it took 15 to 20 minutes for the procedure to be completed in relation to each bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Whilst the people were being beaten from the buses in front of you, what were the two JNA soldiers from Vukovar Hospital, the ones that were guarding you on the bus, what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. They were simply with us on the bus. I don't even think that they left the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what happened to you? After you saw these other buses being unloaded, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: It was my bus's turn. Our turn came, we were unloaded off the bus in the same way. We moved closer to the hangar, and then we were taken off the bus, and then one by one we would walk in the column towards the entrance of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you got near the entrance, what happened?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Before I even reached the entrance I had established contact. I started talking to a soldier there. Then it was my turn to go through the same procedure. I had a rosary around my neck. They pulled it off. I had a wallet with the photographs of my wife and my first child. I had to throw it on the ground. I also had some money, I had to take it out. And I was beaten just like everybody else was in the column. And following that, I entered the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said you made contact with a soldier. Can you explain what that contact was?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Once we got off the bus, there were other soldiers there who took us over and they questioned people. Maybe not everybody, but every second or third person they questioned. They wanted to know everything, what we were doing in Vukovar and so on. This is how the soldier came to ask me where I was from, and this is how we established communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you explain what the nature of that discussion was, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: He asked me, "Where are you from?" I told him I was from Zagreb. Then he asked me, "What are you doing here? What made you come here?" I just shrugged my shoulders. And he responded to me, "I just have few more days left to serve in the army, and then I go back to regular life. I go back to Ruma." Once he mentioned that he was from Ruma, I told him that before the war I used to go to Ruma often, and that I had a friend there. Then he asked me about the friend, and I told him that his nickname was Kemo. He asked me about where he lived, and I told him that I thought it was a street called Partizanskih Odreda or something similar, to which he replied that he knew the person. I was getting closer to the gauntlet, and the moment when I would be beaten was approaching. And I remember saying to him, "Can you please get me out, can you rescue me?" He replied something to this effect: "No chance." Then I entered the gauntlet, went through the procedure that I've already described, and went inside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you describe what this soldier looked like, his age, say the colour of his hair, and what he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I told him that he was approximately -- I remember that he was approximately my age. I know for a fact that he was a regular JNA soldier. He told me himself that he had just a few more days to serve and then he would be going back to Ruma. He was my height. I remember that he had brown hair, a short cut. And he was also clean-shaven. I can't remember whether he was actually clean-shaven or he didn't yet have a proper beard. I also know that he had an oval-shaped face.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you were 20 years old, is that right, at that time?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: At the time I was 21, because my birthday is in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And your height is approximately, in centimetres?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: 175 centimetres exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was this soldier wearing, what type of pants and jacket, the colour?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that he had a coat. I will use the term that we use for that jacket in Croatia, spitfire jacket. It was a short, green-coloured jacket. I can't remember what kind of trousers he wore. I know that he had a so-called pump-action gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was it a military jacket or a civilian jacket; do you know?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: It was a civilian jacket. I never saw such a jacket before as part of a military uniform. In my view, it was a civilian jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the jacket, was it above the belt line, or below it, or on the belt line?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: It was above the belt line. It was a bomber-type jacket, the one that pilots wear. And it was of a similar military-type green colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And at some time later, whilst you were at Ovcara, did this person tell you his name?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: This was afterwards. When they started beating me in the hangar, this person returned to the hangar with some superior officer whom he addressed as Captain. They had just started beating me when he approached me with the captain. He took my shoulder, and I remember him saying, "Captain, let's save this man." The captain said to him, "Take him out, open the door" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, "Take him out next to the door."

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: "And protect him from Chetniks so that they don't kill him."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did he take you outside of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he took me out of the hangar. As we were leaving the hangar at the very entrance, this is not great distance, he hugged me and asked me, "What's your name? What's your name so that I will know, so I will say that we know each other from before." Something to that effect. I told him my name and then I asked him about his name. He said that his name was Stuka, or rather that this is how he was called. That was his nickname. And then I asked him about his proper name. And he said Ilija. That was a brief response. Then he stood with me in front of the hangar the entire time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Perhaps if we can just go back a little bit now to the time that you went through the gauntlet. You said you were beaten. Can you explain what type of beating you received on the way into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I was beaten just like everyone else. The beating did not take long. They kicked me, hit me with their hands, they also hit me with some firm object on my head and on my back, and after that I entered the hangar. They also spat on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Apart from the people, the soldiers involved in the beating in the gauntlet, which -- of which you said there were about 30, were there any other soldiers outside of the hangar as you went in?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: The JNA soldiers were the most numerous ones, at least I identified them as the JNA soldiers. They stood around the hangar securing the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how many did you see at the time that you were going into the hangar before you were beaten? How many of these JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I could see some 15 to 20 soldiers standing on the other side of the road and securing the area. That's what I could see. To tell you the truth, I was not able to observe the situation for a long time, because I also, at the same time, talked to Stuka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Once you arrived inside the hangar, you said that you were beaten again. About how long after you went inside the hangar were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: In the hangar I wasn't beaten badly. It lasted just a couple of minutes, three to four minutes, because Stuka came into the hangar quite shortly after me. He came in together with his superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you referred to this superior officer a moment ago as a captain. Can you explain how you knew that it was a superior officer?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that, but he enabled Stuka to take me out, based on which I concluded that he was his superior officer. I also heard him address the man as Captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was this captain wearing?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that he had a camouflage uniform top, and a dark beret, dark blue beret, with a five-pointed star. He also had a moustache.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And which group would you place him in? You referred to Chetniks, reservists, TOs, regular JNA, or would you place him in another group? Which group would you place that person in?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I would describe him as a JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You were in the hangar only for a short time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you were inside the hangar, could you tell the Court what you saw?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I saw people standing next to the wall. Some of them were lying on the floor. I also saw people beating these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many people did you see in the hangar when you went in on the first occasion?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Altogether, some 200 people, 200 of us and about 40 or so people beating us. I know that there were fewer of them than those who were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you describe the 40 or so that were beating people inside the hangar? Which groups do you think they belonged to, from what you saw?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Based on what I saw, and based on my thoughts about what group they could have belonged to, I can tell you that in the hangar it was a mixed group that did the beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And that mixed group comprised of who?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Chetniks, TO men, and the JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And before you left the hangar about how many other people did you see being beaten, obviously other than yourself?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I saw several people lying on the floor. It would be difficult to put a figure, but it was definitely more than five people that I saw lying on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you see other people actually being beaten whilst you were in the hangar or not?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how many people?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Once you entered the hangar all of the people on the enemy side who had captured us were, for the most part, beating the prisoners who were in the hangar, and this was an all-out fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were the people being beaten, were they resisting?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody resisted. No resistance whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said you were in the hangar for a short time, and then you were taken outside by this person called Stuka. When you got outside what did you see, and who were you with?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Once I went outside some of the people who were driven away together with me were already outside. They had already been rescued, just like I was. Therefore, I saw them, I saw the soldiers who continued standing in front of the hangar with their weapons securing the area. They were the JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many people were rescued like yourself? How many were in that group?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: There were seven of us who were rescued from the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I would ask that we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in public session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how long were you outside of the hangar before something else happened of significance?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: We must have been outside the hangar for at least an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And during that hour, what was happening outside of the hangar? What were you doing, you and your group?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: We weren't doing anything. We were just standing there, waiting for something to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And this soldier called Stuka, what was he doing? Was he there for the whole time?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: He was guarding us throughout. He wasn't alone. There were other soldiers with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: During this hour, about how many other soldiers were outside of the hangar, approximately?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: There were three other men guarding us with Stuka. And there were at least about 15 other men, JNA soldiers carrying weapons, securing the entrance to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Outside did there appear to be anyone in command of these soldiers or not?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: There were certainly people there who were commanders, who had command over those people. A little later, while I was still outside, a group of officers arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how did they arrive, how did they get to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: They arrived in a vehicle. The vehicle drove past Ovcara and parked a little further off.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you describe the type of vehicle it was?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: It was what is usually referred to as a Pinzgauer. It's a rather small all-terrain vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you remember the colour?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Standard JNA; olive-drab.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say a group of officers arrived, about how many, and can you say which military grouping they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: There were three or four. They were wearing JNA uniforms with long coats. There was something that happened afterwards that led me to conclude that one of them was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you explain what that was?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Soon after the officers arrived outside the hangar, a lady appeared from somewhere. She was sobbing and begging this man, who I later learned to be a colonel, to save her son and take him away from the hangar. I remember she was telling him that his [sic] son was a handicapped person and that he was suffering from some sort of congenital deficiency. He went into the hangar with her and brought the boy out of the hangar. I remember that he told her, "There, leave this place and remember one thing. Your son's life was saved by Colonel," and now I can't remember the last name. Ivankovic, Ivanovic, possibly Jovanovic. I can't remember exactly what the last name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you believe that he was referring to himself?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: That was my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to that lady and that boy?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And those officers that arrived, how long did they stay there for?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: They were there throughout, even after I'd left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What happened to the buses? Did they stay at Ovcara or did they leave at some stage? And if they did, when did they leave?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: In order to leave the people there, the buses would drive by, wait for the people to get off, turn around and probably drive straight back to Vukovar. They didn't linger in the area. They left very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned this military vehicle arriving. Were there any other vehicles, either civilian or military, outside of the hangar whilst you were waiting outside?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: There were. I remember one armoured combat vehicle and another light one, a light armoured combat vehicle. One has wheels and the other has a Caterpillar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know which group -- groups those vehicles may have belonged to?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Those were JNA vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what did those officers do whilst you were there, the ones that arrived?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part they were inside the hangar, just standing there. I remember one thing: When a truck drove up to collect our clothing that we had laid down on the ground in a pile, the Chetniks ran to grab as many of the clothes as was possible. One of these officers came out of the hangar and yelled at them, "Why are you touching these? These are Ustashas' things and they are cursed. They should be incinerated and left well alone."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did they continue to grab the belongings or did they leave them after that?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: They left them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did those officers go inside the hangar or did they stay outside, apart from the colonel who you said went inside?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part they stayed inside. A colonel came out once and another man came out at one point to yell at the Chetniks, who were trying to take as many clothes as they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Whilst you were staying outside of the hangar for the hour or so, was the hangar door open or shut, generally?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the door wasn't open wide like earlier on. It was ajar, but not entirely shut.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And could you see or hear what was happening inside the hangar whilst you were outside?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't see anything, but I could hear what was happening. I was able to hear what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what could you hear?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I heard people being beaten throughout. People moaning, people crying for help, people screaming, people sobbing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Whilst you were outside the hangar, this soldier that introduced himself as Ilija with his nickname Stuka, did he communicate with you? Did you talk?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the subject of the conversation? What did he say and what did you say?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I remember I asked him at one point, "What will become of us, what will become of all these people?" And he said, "They will kill you all." He told me again that he only had several days to go before his military term was over. And again we talked about that friend of mine. I explained yet again who he was. I told him I was married and had a son, and that my wife was now carrying another man's child.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, my wife was now pregnant again.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: That is all I remember, but we did talk quite a bit. I was wearing those Canadian-style yellow boots. He told me to take them off because they might cost me my life. I did as he told me to do, and he went to the pile of clothes lying on the ground and found a different pair of shoes for me that were not the same as the yellow Canadian boots, which were popularly referred to as the ZNG boots. He went back to that pile of clothing on the ground and pulled out some sort of a leather jacket which he gave me to wear. I remember him telling me to take off my wedding ring, too, which I had forgot to lay down on the ground previously. He told me the Chetniks might even go as far as cut my finger off just because of that ring. I took it off and I asked him to have it. At first he refused to take my wedding ring. I pleaded with him, saying, "It's better off on you than with me discarding it. Who knows, for all we know, some day you might have a chance to give it back to me." He then took my ring and placed it on one of his fingers. I'm not sure whether it was on the right hand or the left hand, but I know his fingers were thicker than mine, and he placed my wedding ring on his small finger. That's as much as I can remember right now concerning the conversation between Stuka and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And after that hour or so, did you go back into the hangar or did you leave from there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: We returned to the hangar once more. They were beginning to compile a list of people in the hangar. There were seven of us who entered briefly. They took our personal details, first name, last name, father's name, after which we were again taken out, and several minutes later were driven away from Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who was taking the details? Can you describe the people, the person that was taking the details?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I know they were from the JNA, but I can't describe the particular person. I don't remember at all what this person looked like who took our names down. And in addition to that, there were several people standing around that desk. There were those officers present too who had arrived earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What were they writing the names into? Was it on a scrap of paper or a book, or can you describe what they were writing in?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember what sort of paper, scrapbook or notebook they were using. I don't remember anything at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were they just taking your group's details, or did they appear to be taking the details of others inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: They were taking everybody's details. When we entered the hangar there was a group of about seven, eight, or possibly nine people lined up already, people from the hangar and they were taking their details, and we were next.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did they tell you why they were taking the details?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody told us. Nobody told us anything at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
