utterances.text: And when you returned into the hangar after this hour or so, what did you see inside the hangar? You said earlier that people were being beaten the first time. What did you see on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: There were no longer any people being beaten, but I did see a number of people lying on the floor. Some were sitting up and some were just prone. There were some who were standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was your overall impression as to what was happening at the hangar for the time that you were there? Was it chaos, was it orderly? Can you explain the type of situation that you thought was there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: There were 250 people inside the hangar, and if you consider the way we had been brought there and the treatment that we had suffered and the way the situation inside the hangar had been organised, my impression at least was that the order of all these actions, the sequence, was clear enough to them. I think in that sense there was order, yes. The only chaos there were the beatings themselves. It took at least an hour, but possibly more. There was at least an hour of continuous beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe the physical characteristics of the colonel, the colonel that you saw that helped the woman with her boy? What colour was his hair, was he tall or short? How old was he?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: He was taller than me. Which is not a particular feat. He must have been at least 185 centimetres tall. He was at least 10 centimetres taller than I was. Hair greying; on the side at least I think the hair was grey. His face, quite clean, orderly, clean-shaven. I remember he wore the coat draped around his shoulders. As for his hair, there were dark patches and grey patches, that's one thing I remember. Quite vociferous too; his voice struck me as quite loud. He was wearing a JNA uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how old was he?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I think he may have been between 40 and 45 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you describe how you left Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Stuka and another three soldiers escorted a group of seven of us to a white van. They drove us back to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: These three soldiers, do you know which group they belonged to from the groups you've described already?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: They were all regular JNA soldiers. I know that one of them even said he was from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did any of them or anyone else tell you where they were taking you and why you were being taken?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Stuka and this friend of his - he did tell me his nickname, which I've forgot - told us that they were taking us to a place where we'd be safe. They also said that we would soon be exchanged. I remember that Stuka and his friend even gave me a bit of money to have on my way back to Croatia. They didn't tell me exactly the name of the place that they were taking us to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Where were you first taken when you were taken back to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: First they took us to Velepromet. We stayed briefly, several minutes perhaps. We were then driven on to Modateks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was that the first time that you had been to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who told you that that was, in fact, Velepromet, where you were taken first?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I think Cakalic or Berghofer, because one of them knew what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you go inside of Velepromet or not? Was the vehicle parked outside?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we drove straight into Velepromet's courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were you told why you were taken from Velepromet to Modateks, the reason why you left there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't told exactly why, but I imagined what the reason was for us being taken to Modateks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What did you believe the reason to be?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Stuka and his friend had previously told me that they would take us somewhere from where we could be sent back to Croatia immediately. At Modateks there were elderly people, women and children, and in actual fact those were the groups that were being sent back to Croatia. So that was probably the reason. Stuka and his friends probably intended to help me all the way, help me as much as they could. However, not even he knew what the odds were or the entire situation that prevailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you left Ovcara, can you tell the Court whether it was light or dark or getting dark, or do you know the time?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I know that it was getting dark. It was just before nightfall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you stay the night at Modateks?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was anyone guarding these elderly people, women and children, in that place?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were soldiers of the JNA there. There was a rather senior man commanding them, whom they were calling Deda, or grand-dad.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did anything happen during the night whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: That night a group of Chetniks arrived. They toured the entire Modateks compound, which is where we were being kept. They reached our group, the seven of us. They called this man called Deda over to explain to them what we were doing there. When he explained the matter, they said there was not a cat's chance us being sent on that bus to that exchange. Just before daybreak, it was still dark, all the civilians, the women, the elderly, the children, left on buses, I believe that between 70 and 100 people were taken away. The seven of us remained inside this factory hall. Early the next morning Deda told us to clean the place up. I must say that both Deda and the other soldiers there were quite fair or respectful. They allowed us to eat some canned food and they gave us water to drink. Actually, that morning, as we were still cleaning that hall, this group of Chetniks returned to check if we were still there. Deda told them that he needed us to clean the place up. When the Chetniks left and we finished our job, Deda and several other soldiers led our group, the seven of us, to Velepromet. We walked to Velepromet. I remember Deda saying that we should be taken away as soon as possible before the Chetniks were back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What happened to the three soldiers and this Stuka, what happened to them? Did they --

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: They went back to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That was after taking you to Modateks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was the night they left us at Modateks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Have you ever seen that Stuka again since that day?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What happened to you when you got to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: We came to the yard of Velepromet, and Deda handed us over to a military police officer, commander. We were searched once again there in Velepromet, and then we were sent to a room in a building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who were they, the military -- who was this military police officer from, what group?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how did you know he was a military police officer?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: He had white belt; that's what they normally wear. I know that they also had white batons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how many people did the searching of you and your group?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Seven or eight, because there was a total of perhaps 10 of them, the military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you first arrived at Velepromet, other than the military police you saw there, were there any other soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the yard there were JNA soldiers, TO men. I think that there were even two or three Chetniks. There weren't too many soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About what time did you arrive at Velepromet that day? And I think it's the 21st of November.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the 21st of November. I could have arrived in Velepromet at around 11.00 or 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that you were sent to a room in a building. Can you describe the type of building and how you got into that particular room?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was a one-storey building. It just had the ground floor. Once you enter the Velepromet complex, you face that room immediately. I learned later that it was known as the carpentry workshop, and this room -- or, rather, there were several rooms, one was on the left and one was on the right. I went to the one on the left. In that central room there was a table, and this commander was in this room.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said the commander was in this room. Was there anyone else in that room, in that central room when you walked into the room you were placed in?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: There were several soldiers, military policemen of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said there was seven of you in the group. Did you all go to the same room, or did you go to different rooms?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't all go to the same room. We were assigned to separate rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What did you see when you went into your room?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I saw at least 20 to 25 people there in the room sitting with concerned expressions on their faces, mostly men, some of them were senior. And I remember that there was a young boy there in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What type of clothing were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: All of them had civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: From being in that room with them, were you able to find out what their ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How long were you in that room before you left it?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Several hours. Five or six hours, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What happened during that five or six hours?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: For a while, nothing happened. Then they started entering our room, the Chetniks, and selecting people and taking them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many people were taken out of your room before you were taken out?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: What I remember is that three persons were taken out before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who were they? Can you describe them?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I remember a man who was older than me. He was around 40. He was taken out the first. And then I remember that Perkovic, who had arrived with me from Ovcara, was taken out. And then this youngish boy was taken out, also before me. He could have been 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You have said that Chetniks took these people out. Did they take them out separately or together?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Separately. Individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how many Chetniks were coming in and taking out these three people?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: There were two groups of Chetniks. One group came in once, and the second group twice. They would come in in twos, once the military policemen let them in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you explain what happened when the young boy was taken out, the circumstances that were occurring in the room?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: The Chetniks entered the room. First they selected his brother, who was with him in the room and who was older than him. He was around my age, the brother. The Chetnik whom I remember had some kind of a knife or a dagger in his hand and he pointed with it to the brother, after which the younger brother started crying and pleading, "Not my brother, please, not my brother." Then the Chetnik said to the older brother that he could sit down, he didn't need to leave. And then he pointed to the younger brother, indicating that he should go out with him. Once they left the room we heard him say to the boy to take his clothes off. After several minutes we could hear this sound coming from behind us. We heard crying, yelling, pleading, screaming. Unnatural sounds uttered by the boy. That lasted some 15 minutes or so, 20 minutes. I remember that he begged them not to do that to him, that it hurt him a lot. After 15 to 20 minutes, shots were heard. And then the sounds coming from the boy ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was there a window in your room to the outside?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a window. Which was somewhat higher, we couldn't see through it. There was a window, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what about the circumstances surrounding the 40-year-old and this Perkovic that was taken out? With either of them did you hear anything after they were taken out of your room or not?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: It progressed in a similar way. I know that Perkovic explained to the Chetnik who took him out that he had been saved by the son of Dr. Ivankovic. I know that he also told him, "Please don't do this. What are you doing to me?" Or rather, "Why are you doing this to me?" However, they went further away from the room so that we couldn't hear the entire conversation or exchange. But I also heard him moaning. The three men taken out before me were treated in a similar way, the way they were taken out, and treated afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that when the young boy was taken out you heard crying and pleading, and then shortly after that you heard gunshots. Did you hear that in relation to these men, or is that something you didn't hear?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: In all three cases everything would end with shots. Whether all of them were killed by shots, whether they died, I don't know. The fact is that no further sounds were heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What about people in the other room?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, I think we might break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If that's convenient. The witness has been in the box for a long session, and we need to change the tapes. We will resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, before we had a break you explained how two men and a boy were taken out of the room that you were in and before you were taken out yourself. And you said that one of those men had the name of Perkovic. In a statement that you gave to the Prosecution on the 16th of January, 2006 you stated that Perkovic was, in fact, in the other room, not in the room that were you in. Can you explain why you think today that Perkovic was in the room that you were in?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, I remember when that Chetnik came to get him, he knew him and he called out his last name, Perkovic. Recently at the Belgrade trial I believe I also stated that Perkovic was in the same room as I.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you were taken out of the room at Velepromet. Who took you out and where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I was taken out by a group of Chetniks who had previously not been around, or they hadn't taken anyone out before they took me out, this third group. They took me out of that room, and I remember that I was sitting there when one of the Chetniks entered the room and addressed me, "You, good-looking lad over there with black hair, come over." I was in the process of rising from the floor and I had a jacket draped over my shoulders. The jacket fell down to the ground. I wanted to put it back on, and then he told me, "You won't be needing that one anymore. Just leave it be." After this I left the room and they took me through the rear part of this small building. We left the building, we crossed some sort of a courtyard, and this man told me that we were going to see some sort of a major for some questioning. It was from the courtyard that we reached a narrow road, and I remember that there were rail tracks nearby. We walked on for about 100 or 200 metres down that road. We reached a crossing when a vehicle appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you were taken out of the room, did you see any military police on the way out or not?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Military police were there throughout. They were opening and closing the door to that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How many Chetniks took you to this road?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when the car appeared, what happened?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I was put into that vehicle and driven to a house. We drove for a very short time, perhaps two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Before we talk briefly about what happened at that house, if I could ask the usher to place Exhibit 262 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, do you see the buildings on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what do you recognise those buildings as?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were taken into a carpentry workshop. Do you see that on the -- within the Velepromet compound there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, would you be able to circle the carpentry workshop, please?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I seek to tender that photograph, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 293, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if I could call for the next exhibit, 156, please. And if I could ask that the Velepromet photograph be enlarged, please, as much as you can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, looking at this photograph here, do you recognise the building within that photograph?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what is that -- what is that a -- what's the name of that building?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: This is the so-called carpentry workshop.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: With the pen, if you could circle the entrance you went through to get to your room, please.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you can mark that with an A. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The room that you went into, can you see that in the photograph, or at least the outside wall of it?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you circle the area where that room is, please?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you can mark that with a B.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the other room where the other people were placed into, could you circle that, or at least the outside wall of that room, and mark that with a C, please?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I seek to tender that photograph, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number 294.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I would just call for the last exhibit on this point, Exhibit 256, photograph 16, please. And if the bottom left-hand corner, if that could be enlarged, please. Thank you. That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, do you see the photograph on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to see the carpentry workshop in that photograph that you were placed in?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you can circle that and mark it with an A, please.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Whilst you have the pen in your hand, could you show, with a line, please, the route that you took when you were taken by the Chetniks and placed in the car near the -- near the railway line?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I seek to tender that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number 295.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: We have finished with this exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, you said you were taken to a house by these Chetniks, and when you got to the house, can you tell the Court what happened there, just briefly? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: When I came to that house there were about 20 Chetniks there. At first everybody seemed happy that I was brought to the house. I know that the man who brought me there, whose nickname was Belgija, spat in my face and cursed me in our usual Balkan way. He was telling me that I would now see for myself what Chetniks could do. They sat me down in the middle of a table. To my left there was Belgija, and to my right there was a man seated there who was quite a bit older, wearing a Chetnik uniform with all the Chetnik insignia. Behind me there was a man nicknamed Cedo standing, pointing a rifle at the small of my neck. They started questioning me and beating me. They stripped the clothes that I had on top. And then Belgija tried to use a lighter to set my hair on fire. However, it was a very humid day, a very humid evening, and my hair was wet and wouldn't catch fire. Belgija then tried to burn my left arm with this lighter. He didn't seem to be doing too well with that lighter, so he picked up a candle from the table and pressed it against my left ear. I couldn't take the pain, and I had not been restrained. So I instinctively warded off the candle with my hand, which was reason enough for both Belgija and this man to start hitting me. Across the way at the table there was a woman wearing a "sajkaca," Chetnik cap. She asked the Chetniks to rape me, saying that she would then slice my genitals off. Meanwhile, there was another man in the room, actually I mentioned this man, this older man who was seated to my right. At one point Belgija again grabbed the candle and started burning my left nipple with the candle. I couldn't take this pain for very long, so again I flailed my arm, throwing the candle to the floor. This older Chetnik who was there picked a bottle off the table and cracked me over the head with this bottle, smashing the bottle in the process and using the remaining part of the bottle that he was still holding to cut me across my arms and back. After this, both Belgija and Cedo hit me again. I fell off the chair and fell on the floor. So they kicked me some more. I remember that this woman who was with them kept pressing them to rape me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you raped?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: No. At this point what happened was the reason that I testified in Belgrade recently. Two men came into the room. I can say now, because I know, what their names were. Kinez and Mare. A huge quarrel erupted between them and the Chetniks, especially this Chetnik called Belgija. I remember Kinez telling the Chetniks as follows: "Belgija, did you capture this man? What makes you think you have the right to treat POWs like this?" He asked him several times, "Did you capture this man at the front line?" I was across the table at this point in time, so Kinez walked all the way around. He grabbed my right arm in a bid to drag me out of the room and away from those people. This is what the situation was. Kinez, as far as I remember, was carrying an automatic rifle, and Mare had a handgun, a pistol, while the Chetniks were all armed. So they held each other at gunpoint, and Kinez eventually dragged me out of the house and into the yard. He stood in front of me. I had both Mare and Kinez standing in front of me, shielding me as it were, at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for that. The full name of Kinez and Mare, do you know their full names?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Kinez's name is Predrag Milojevic. Milojevic, Milojevic not Mihaljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And Mare's full name?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Mare is Marko Ljuboja.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And is it the case that Mare's defence lawyer contacted you to give evidence in the trial at Belgrade that both of those were standing as accused in?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And both of those two were charged with the killings at Ovcara, is that correct, in the Belgrade trial.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the outcome of that trial for both of those two? Were they found guilty or innocent?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Luckily Marko Ljuboja was acquitted on all counts for Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And Kinez?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: And Predrag Milojevic, a.k.a. Kinez, was unfortunately convicted and got the maximum penalty; 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, these two men that saved you, they took you to another house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: We first came to another house and entered the garden in front of that house. There was a JNA officer standing in that garden as well as a lady. They gave me some water to drink and gave me an apple to eat. They also gave me some sort of a JNA shirt to put on, since I was naked from the waist up. At this point in time Belgija came after us again. He came into that garden and wanted to speak to Kinez. He told Kinez to give me back to them, explaining that I would be the last man that he would be taking care of. Kinez refused flat out and told him in a very sharp voice to leave this place and go away. I never entered the house but was taken from the garden to a different house. I realised that there were military policemen staying at the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long did you stay at this place, and where were you taken after that?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I could have stayed there for some 15 minutes while they got organised. There was an officer with them, a captain. That was his rank. I didn't see any military police insignia on him. This officer and some three to four military policemen, Kinez and Mare, went into an APC together with me, an armoured combat vehicle, and went back to Ovcara. No, I apologise, went back to Velepromet, I apologise. To the same place, the carpentry workshop.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And these four military policemen which group did they belong to, of the ones you've described, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when they took you to Velepromet, what happened there, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: A great argument broke out there between the military policemen who, under quotation mark, looked after the people there at Velepromet on one hand, and Kinez and Mare, particularly Mare, on the other hand. What happened was that they pulled out weapons at each other. And then the officer intervened, the captain, who calmed the situation down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why were the weapons pulled out between Kinez and Mare and this military policeman from Velepromet, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mare started cursing immediately at this military policeman, and I guess he was offended by it, so this is why they pulled out weapons at each other. I know that Mare was wounded in his left arm, and I know that he said to the man, "I don't need any weapons. Come out outside and I will fight you with one arm." As for Kinez, and even Mare, they kept saying the entire time that that was no way to treat POWs and how they believed that they had right to do something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How long did you stay at Velepromet before you were taken somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: For another hour and a half to two hours perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you go back to the same room that you originally were in before you were taken out?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were there people still in that room or not?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Whilst you were at Velepromet, were you taken to the doctor for injuries you received?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: After some time, since I was exhausted, I was lying in that room. And then I heard the door open again and I heard a deep voice of a man who asked, "Where is this man who was cut or cut up?"

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. If I can just cut you short just a little bit. Did you receive some treatment at Velepromet from someone there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after that, once I got up, I introduced myself as the person he was looking for. This is why I told you this whole introduction. This man and another soldier, who was a part of his security detail, took me out of the room and then he said to the soldier to take me to the doctor. After that I received medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then did a bus arrive at Velepromet and were you and others taken somewhere?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: A bus arrived at Velepromet. All of the people from those two rooms entered the bus. I remember that I and the soldier who was part of the security detail, as well as the man in charge, the man of authority for whom I later learned that he was the commander of the barracks, got into his personal car, which was an Opel Omega. I also remember that when I entered the car I saw a watch in front -- or, rather, a clock. And I remember what time it was. And this car took us further on to the same place where the bus went.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where was that? Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: We were taken to the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at Velepromet, when you returned after being beaten up and you went back to your room, was Perkovic there, was that young boy there, and was that 40-year-old man, were they still in the room? Did they return to the room or not after they had been taken out?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't come back. Nobody returned. I didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was -- when you got to the barracks, did you stay there that night?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We stayed the night at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And at the barracks were you guarded at all?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: We were guarded by the troops, the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many people got into the bus and went to the JNA barracks from Velepromet? I know you went in a separate vehicle, but can you say?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Some 60 people. I know this on the basis of the fact that the bus was full, and some people also stood on the bus. We drove in parallel to the barracks. Once we arrived to that room in the barracks, we found some 15 people there who had nothing to do with Velepromet. There were even some women there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you discuss with any of these other people that were detained at Velepromet with you, either in your room or the other room, as to what happened to people at Velepromet that day on the 21st of November?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: That night in the barracks we were able to talk to each other. Because we were in that room and were free to talk. Based on those conversations, I learned that we were in the Vukovar barracks and that a total of some 15 men had been taken out on that day and that I was the only one to return alive to the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: 15 men had been taken out of where?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: From Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The next day did you leave the JNA barracks and go to Sremska Mitrovica? This is on the 22nd of November.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who took you to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How did you get there, how did the 60 of you get there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: In a bus. We called that articulated bus, and there were some 75 to 80 people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So is that like two buses joined together?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: It looks as a bus and a half, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was that bus guarded?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There were soldiers on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How long did you stay at Sremska Mitrovica, and where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I spent six months in Sremska Mitrovica, and then following that I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you were taken to a civilian prison there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you ever charged with anything, with any offence whilst in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Whilst you were at that prison, were you ever interviewed about your involvement in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many times were you interviewed over that six-month period?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Eight to 10 times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who was conducting the interviews?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: The JNA. I don't know the names of the people who interviewed me. For the most part, they were all different people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say the JNA, was it the military police in the JNA, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: The military police of the JNA guarded us. We were interviewed by the JNA officers. They didn't have military police insignia, and there was nothing on the basis of which I could have concluded that they were members of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And briefly, what was the focus of the interviews? What types of questions were they?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: The questions mostly required me to explain what we did, how we did it. Mostly those kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And during these interviews, how were you treated?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: On two or three occasions I was treated well. As for the other five or six cases, I was beaten. On another two occasions I was beaten, and that had nothing do with the questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you have said that you were released on the 22nd of May, 1992. Was that a part of a prisoner exchange?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that was part of exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, I briefly would like to discuss, run through a couple of points in relation to statements that you've given, either the Tribunal, the OTP or testimonies at the Tribunal, and if you can just confirm whether this is correct or not. In 1995 you gave a statement to Tribunal investigators. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in March 1996 you testified in a hearing at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then in 1998 you testified in the Dokmanovic case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And last year, in 2005, you testified at the Belgrade trial for accused involved in the events at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then you gave a statement to ICTY investigators in January 2006?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just my last topic. Before you testified at the hearing in 1996 at the Tribunal, did you contact the military security services in the army in Zagreb about that testimony?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because that was my duty. And as a soldier I, of course, had to get in touch with my security services.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you got in touch with them, what transpired?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing came out of it. I simply told my story, I told them about what had happened, because prior to that I had never discussed it with anybody in Croatia. As a soldier, I am unable to seek protection from civilian police. This is why there exists security service, and they take care of security of the soldiers. You have to realise that I felt unsafe when the people from other country contacted me about retelling these events to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And is it correct that you spoke to someone from the security services over a two-day period for about three hours a day?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you told them about the events in Vukovar and Ovcara; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did they ask you any questions about what you told them?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: They did when they wanted to clarify some things. It is hard to understand my story unless you hear it for several times or unless you experienced it personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did they tell you what you should say or how you should give your testimony at the Tribunal in that case in 1996?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. Mr. Vasic. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, it's me. [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see that we have eight minutes left. If you think that I should begin, I will. But I would rather leave it for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will take you in good faith, Mr. Domazet, in the expectation borne out of experience, that tomorrow will be quicker if you are able to collect your thoughts. We would hope that the evidence of the witness might be concluded tomorrow. So if you would sharpen your attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I hope so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Allowing plenty of room for your colleagues to follow, plenty of time. We will adjourn now for the evening and continue tomorrow at 2.15 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
